summary: Agriculture innovation money is flowing to tools that cut input costs on existing farms: Deere's camera sprayers (5 million acres in 2025), biological fertilizers, and gene editing now that the EU has passed light-touch rules and the US approved a PRRS-resistant pig. Venture money has fled lab-grown meat and vertical farms after billions in losses. The farm equipment cycle is at a bottom in 2026, so tech adoption is coming from retrofits and pay-per-acre models, not new machine sales. Corteva completed its split on Oct 1, 2026: seeds and gene editing now trade as Vylor (VYLR), while crop protection and biologicals stay in Corteva (CTVA). Fertilizer stayed costly through the Hormuz disruption (US retail urea about $655 a ton in early September 2026), which keeps the cost case for nitrogen-fixing microbes alive. Retrofit autonomy is where the new launches are: Deere and AGCO both showed new kits in early October 2026. AGCO's Q3 (Oct 29) showed the equipment slump is not over: sales fell 8.6%, Brazil tractor retail sales were down 17% for nine months, and it targets about $1 billion of PTx precision sales this year and $2 billion by 2029.

latest_change.what: Rechecked on the daily rotation. AGCO's Q3 (Oct 29) sales fell 8.6% to $2.26 billion, with Latin America down 19.1% and Brazil tractor retail sales down 17% for nine months; it kept its 2026 outlook and targets $2 billion of PTx retrofit sales by 2029 from about $1 billion this year. About 29% of global urea trade normally passes Hormuz (S&P Global), which keeps the cost case for nitrogen-fixing biologicals alive. No stage moves: the PRRS pig still waits on Mexico and Japan, and Corteva reports Nov 11.
latest_change.for_you: No action on AGCO or DE; neither has a buy zone verdict, and AGCO's sales are still falling. CF is 'Buy zone now' (119.92 on Oct 28, Massive) and benefits from tight nitrogen, but it reports Nov 4 after the close (company release), inside any new put window, so no put now. Mark Nov 11 for Corteva.

summary: The biggest new money in communications is AI traffic between data centers: Lumen has about $13B of AI fiber contracts and Ciena expects more than $10B of backlog, which is more certain than anything in consumer telecom. Space is the second flow: SpaceX (SPCX) closed at about a $2.26T market value on Oct 5, 2026, Starlink Mobile reached about 22M monthly users by August, and Amazon is spending to catch up (Leo plus an $11.6B Globalstar deal). All 56 state BEAD broadband plans are now approved, so rural fiber money moves from paperwork to construction. Open RAN and AI-RAN are still trials. Ericsson grew sales 7% organically in Q3 2026 but still expects a flat radio market this year.

innovations.name: AI data center interconnect (long haul fiber and coherent optics)

latest_change.what: Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum for $115 billion in stock, combining Marvell's electrical chips with Lumentum's lasers and optics for AI data centers. Marvell says the deal lifts its addressable market to $550 billion (company release via CNBC, Nov 2). It is the largest bet yet that optical links become the chokepoint inside AI clusters.
latest_change.for_you: No action today. MRVL holders pay with dilution and the stock is Wait under its zone. COHR is the main independent laser maker left; a buyer paying $115 billion puts a value on its kind of asset. CIEN is left out: it is a customer and a rival. No puts in any of these before the price settles.

summary: Consumer innovation money is flowing to AI glasses and health wearables, but growth is cooling at the top: EssilorLuxottica's wearables revenue was 486 million euros in Q3, about 6.5% of sales, up 20% but a sharp slowdown from earlier quarters (Reuters, Quartz, Oct 20). Oura still has no new IPO date after postponing on September 29. Dexcom grew 11% in Q3 and raised its 2026 guide, so continuous glucose sensing keeps spreading. Cash pay health (GLP-1s through telehealth and direct from the drug maker) is the largest new consumer spend line, and checkout inside AI agents faces its first holiday season.

summary: Defense innovation money is moving from prototypes into first production contracts: the first US laser weapon production deal ($464.8 million to AeroVironment), the first drone wingman jets (General Atomics and Anduril, with Northrop's YFQ-48A now flying), and up to $3.2 billion for space based interceptor prototypes. Cheap mass, meaning drones and the systems that kill drones, gets the fastest growing budgets. The near term brake is Congress: the Pentagon is on a continuing resolution through Dec 11, 2026, which blocks new starts, and Golden Dome's big money depends on a second reconciliation bill. Many of the best positioned builders (Anduril, Castelion, Epirus, General Atomics) are private, so public exposure comes through primes, parts makers and a few volatile small caps.

innovations.name: Hypersonic strike and counter hypersonic defense

latest_change.what: Rechecked on the daily rotation. Enhanced geothermal just crossed into commercial service: Fervo's first 33 MW block at Cape Station, Utah began commercial operation on Sep 30, 2026. Advanced nuclear is building test reactors with first commercial power due 2028 to 2030, and fusion is still a science bet whose public listing (TAE with Trump Media) has not closed.

summary: Financial innovation money is going into new rails for moving dollars: stablecoins (about $312B outstanding on Oct 5, 2026; Treasury's first GENIUS Act rule came Sep 30 and the OCC targets a final rule in November), tokenized assets (about $38.8B on Sep 15; DTCC's tokenization service is due to launch this month), and instant bank payments (FedNow volume up 83% in Q2). The incumbents are buying their way in (Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, BlackRock, DTCC), so the clearest winners so far are the networks and asset managers, not the crypto pure plays. AI in lending and fraud is already paying off in real revenue (Upstart originations up 50%, Mastercard security services leading its fastest-growing segment).

summary: Most of the new money in healthcare is still going to obesity drugs: Lilly raised its 2026 revenue guide to $91 to $92 billion on Oct 29 after Q3 revenue rose 39%, as GLP-1 volume rises while prices fall. Big pharma is also buying one-time genetic medicines (Lilly bought Verve, AbbVie bought Capstan) and the first in vivo CRISPR drug now has an FDA decision date (March 10, 2027), and surgical robots now have US rivals to Intuitive just as its US procedure growth slowed to 10% and it plans to cut instrument revenue per case 3% to 5%. AI diagnostics and brain implants draw heavy venture money, but reimbursement codes, not technology, are what hold them back.

summary: The real money in industrials is going to automation that already pays back: warehouse robots (Symbotic backlog $22.5 billion, now buying cellumation for sortation) and industrial software (Schneider agreed to buy PTC for $205 a share; Siemens bought Altair). Defense is the main buyer pulling industrial 3D printing into real production.

summary: Most new tech money is still AI infrastructure, and the floor is still rising: Meta narrowed 2026 capex to $135 to $145 billion and TSMC guided Q4 revenue to $52.3 to $54.3 billion. What changed in October is how it is paid for: Meta had negative free cash flow in Q3 and is creating a non voting share class to raise money, and every AI report on Oct 21 was sold. The fastest growth is still in inference chips (Broadcom AI chip revenue up 221% y/y) and in parts that are sold out, namely advanced packaging and optics (Nokia AI and cloud sales up 123%). Quantum computing runs on government and equity money (IonQ raised about $2 billion in October), but revenue is still small. Edge AI devices ship in volume (AI PCs are over half of 2026 PC shipments) yet people rarely use the on-device AI.
